newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy March new car registrations leap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy March new car registrations leap.

text.p: Italian new car registrations in March lept 25.04 percent as a government-backed car buying scheme continued to push up demand, while its dominant carmaker Fiat struggled to keep pace with the domestic market.

New registrations rose to 220,500 vehicles in March, compared with 176,348 in March 1996, figures from the Italian Ministry of Transport showed on Thursday. This came after a 21.45 percent year-on-year rise seen in February.
For the three month period January-March 1997, Italian new car registations have risen 16.32 percent to 625,500 vehicles from 537,737 in the period January-March 1996.

Italy launched its car incentive buying scheme in January this year and it is set to run until September. Owners of cars over 10 years old can trade them in to receive a price discount when they buy a new car.

Fiat itself saw a rise of 22.7 percent in its March new car registrations in Italy from March 1996. The group which includes Fiat, Alfa Romeo, Innocenti and Lancia marques struggled to keep up with the higher than expected demand for new cars.

As as consequence, Fiat's share of the Italian new car market fell slightly to 43.55 percent in March from 44.39 percent in March 1996. In February, Fiat car registrations rose 24.2 percent to give it a market share of 44.9 percent.
Fiat recently took on some 2,000 extra workers to meet the surge in new car demand, but only 600 are currently employed while the rest will start work in the coming months.

However, in the rest of Europe Fiat outperformed the market with its sales up 6.8 percent in March year-on-year in an overall European market which fell 3.2 percent, giving Fiat a market share of 12.8 percent against 11.6 percent in March 1996.
The figures confirmed Fiat's second place ranking among European manufacturers behind Germany's Volkswagen.

Italian carmakers' association Anfia said the March new car registrations figures confirmed the effects of the new cars for old scheme and put Italy in line to return to an annual sales volume of some two million vehicles.
"With volumes like these the Italian market is reconfirmed as the second European market after Germany," Anfia said.

Car importing body Unrae also said the incentive scheme had helped the domestic market recover after four depressed years but warned that "this measure alone will not be enough to resolve the structural problems of the sector."
The experience of other European markets, Unrae added, had shown that benefits deriving from incentive schemes should not be overestimated.

Industry analysts also warned what may happen to Italy's car market when the incentive scheme closes later this year, as many purchases had clearly been brought forward to benefit from the scheme which is financed by the government and the industry.
Elsewhere in Europe, the French market in March saw a 20.9 percent slump, German sales fell 9.3 percent and in Britain they slipped 0.8 percent. But the Spanish market grew 1.9 percent.
Cumulative sales for the first quarter showed a 25.5 percent fall in France and a six percent decline in Germany. But the British market rose 3.2 percent and Spain six percent.
